I have been returning to some stuff left by the wayside (like this sub) and have been contacting some people involved with early mainframes, primarily the PLATO network. Even those who know about the ARPANET probably haven't heard of PLATO, so let me try and succinctly explain some of what PLATO is and where you can read more about it.

-PLATO was originally a program, then a network, then a computer line established from the University of Illinois. Here's your quick and dirty Wikipedia entry on its history, though most operative for our purposes is the PLATO IV which was built in 1972 and financed by Control Data Corporation.

-PLATO IV featured a plasma display touch screen monitor which facilitated learning programs. Very quickly, as early as mid 1973, the platform was being overtaken by utility programs and networked multiplayer games. Here's a page dedicated to one of the earliest pure games, Empire which includes some great photos and general knowledge about the PLATO program. Spasim was a widely copied program on the system and was quite possibly the very first game to feature full 360 degrees of 3D movement.

-You can experience PLATO for yourself by going to http://www.cyber1.org/ and signing up for an account on the PLATO emulator. While the games themselves can be obtuse at times, the accessibility is great and there is an actual community using it. You can also check out the PLATO history blog run by Brian Dear, the absolute authority on the PLATO network. His book about the system may be coming next year and I can't wait to read it.

There was also a 50th anniversary PLATO panel at the Computer History Museum that I highly suggest you check out for some greater perspective on both the historical and community side of PLATO.

Speaking of said community, possibly the earliest forum programs was called notes, and the author of that program, Dave Woolley, linked me to the saved archives which date all the way back to 1972 (before he started work on his version of Notes). Once you get into the updated version people start having some very fascinating conversations, both on the level of technology and society. You can see the original message that John Daleske sent to Silas Warner (creator of Castle Wolfenstein) which got them to work on Empire together and discussions of said games later on down the line.

In this particular text you can users welcoming and discussing the ARPANET, but also discussing how difficult gaming would be with a full second of delay time. This is really fascinating not just in terms of the time period but from a programmers perspective. The thought immediately went to real-time programs and games, so that really goes to show how much of a gaming network PLATO was.

This was only a primer on PLATO, as I didn't really have anything to say on it here other than "more people should know about this". I'm hoping that these accomplishments will be recognized and that we can dig up more interesting things about the system and those who worked on it. Bruce Artwick, creator of Flight Simulator, got his start on PLATO, as did Alan McNeil of Berserk fame, Andrew Greenberg used PLATO multiplayer RPGs as a basis for Wizardry, and even creators of the Apple II program Graphics Magician got the initial idea from PLATO's own powerful aesthetics. I might write up some specifics later, but I'd liek to hear your thoughts.
